newsitem.title: FRANCE: France reassures taxpayers on Vendee Globe rescue.
newsitem.headline: France reassures taxpayers on Vendee Globe rescue.

text.p: France's Sports Minister Guy Drut assured taxpayers on Tuesday that they would not have to pay for Australia's dramatic rescue of French yachtsmen in the accident-prone Vendee Globe Challenge solo round-the-world race.
Answering questions in the National Assembly, Drut said rescue operations in the French-organised race were covered by an international convention on rescue at sea.
"The international convention on sea rescue has no bearing on the countries whose boats fly their flag," he said.

Drut said he had written to Australian authorities to congratulate and thank them for the rescue of Frenchman Thierry Dubois and Briton Tony Bullimore whose yachts capsized in a remote Antarctic area.
The costly operation, 1,600 miles (2,400 km) from shore, involved an Australian Navy frigate and tanker, helicopters and planes with sophisticated radar, sonar and camera equipment.

Australia has said the rescue took place in the worst possible circumstances of foul weather and remoteness from land and shipping routes, and had reached virtually the limit of what could be achieved.
Another Frenchman, Raphael Dinelli, was picked up by a fellow-competitor after an Australian air force plane dropped him a life raft minutes before his capsized yacht sank.

In an earlier Vendee Globe Challenge race, Frenchwoman Isabelle Autissier owed her life to a million-dollar Australian Navy rescue operation. She is racing again this year but was disqualified after calling at a South African port for repairs.

Another competitor, Canadian Gerry Roufs, was reported missing almost two weeks ago somewhere between New Zealand, Antarctica and South America. Searches by the Argentine and Chilean military have failed to find any sign of his boat.
The accidents have triggered charges in France that the race was too dangerous and that yacht builders had sacrificed safety to speed.

Competitors, sailing from Vendee in western France, must round the southern tip of Africa, skirt Antarctica eastwards and round Cape Horn at the tip of South America on their way back to the French port of Les Sables d'Olonne.
They are tempted to cut the way short by sailing as close as possible to Antarctica, in lonely, towering seas fraught with dangerous icebergs.
Some critics have suggested that the race's route should be modified to ban competitors from sailing so far south. Others have said it should be abandonned altogether.
Drut said sailors were aware of the risks they were taking and he opposed scrapping the race.
"Do we have the right to go for zero risk, for an aseptic society from which great mountain climbs and motor sports would be banned?" he asked.
But he said organisers and yacht builders would have to take a deep look at the conditions of the next race in order to improve safety.
"Sailors and designers are aware of the need for constructive dialogue so that the race may preserve its reputation with the best guarantees for all," he said.
